name: Praex

hlido_opinion.headline: An open-source, multi-surface coding copartner — terminal, phone and web on one session — that runs on the maker's own models or your keys, and is free to start. The models themselves are the unproven part.
hlido_opinion.body: Praex is an opencode fork (MIT) with a clear, well-stated position: one agent you reach from the terminal, your phone and the web with the same session and memory, running on models the team tunes and serves themselves — 'no middleman' — or on your own keys and hardware if you prefer. The surface is honest about what it is: it names the fork, it lets you start with no sign-up ('press Enter and Velox II answers'), it installs by a single curl line, and it publishes its pricing plainly — Velox II free every day in chat and terminal, Pro at $20 a month for the larger Faber II on demand with five times the daily allowance, and a Max tier (Lucia II) that 'opens soon'. The multi-surface, same-session design is a genuine and uncommon convenience, and being a clean MIT fork means the plumbing is inspectable. The whole value proposition, though, rests on a claim this review cannot test from a public surface: that proprietary models called Velox, Faber and Lucia II are good enough to make 'our own models, no middleman' an advantage rather than a liability. There are no published benchmarks, no model cards, no third-party evaluations, and the strongest external signal — NVIDIA Inception membership — is a startup-program badge, not a quality measure. The top tier is also not fully shipped. So this scores as a competent, honest, usefully-shaped product whose differentiator is unverified: the design and the openness earn real credit, the model quality is a question the buyer has to answer themselves, and the free tier is exactly the right way for them to do it before paying.

tier_rationale: STEADY (73) because the product is live and free to start, the pricing is published and specific ($20/month Pro), it is an MIT fork of opencode so the client is inspectable, the multi-surface same-session design is a real and uncommon convenience, and nothing can be verified or refuted is hidden — the fork, the free entry and the 'opens soon' tier are all stated plainly. Not higher because the central claim — that the maker's own Velox / Faber / Lucia II models are good — carries no public benchmarks, model cards or independent evaluation, the top (Max) tier is not yet shipped, and the team's reach is a single contact address.
what_it_does_well: One copartner across terminal, phone and web with the same session and memory — an uncommon, genuinely useful design
Free to start with no sign-up; Velox II answers immediately in the chat and terminal
Publishes specific pricing: free everyday tier, Pro $20/month for the larger model on demand with 5× the daily allowance
Open source — an MIT fork of opencode — so the client is inspectable, and it supports bringing your own keys or hardware
Clear, unhedged positioning ('answers, not lectures') and a stated privacy-by-design posture
Single-line CLI install and a short demo lower the cost of trying it
what_it_fails_at: The core differentiator — proprietary Velox / Faber / Lucia II models — has no published benchmarks, model cards or third-party evaluation
'Our own models, answerable to no third party' is a strong claim that the public surface gives no way to verify
The Max tier (Lucia II) is advertised as 'opens soon' — not yet shipped
No operating history, uptime or scale evidence; the only contact is a single email address
As an opencode fork, the client-side differentiation over upstream rests almost entirely on the unproven models
NVIDIA Inception is cited as a credential, but it is a startup-program membership, not a measure of model or product quality
best_for: Developers who want one agent spanning terminal, phone and web without re-establishing context
People who want to try a coding copartner free, with no sign-up, before deciding
Users who prefer an open-source client and the option to bring their own model keys or hardware
Privacy-conscious users willing to evaluate the bundled models on their own tasks
not_recommended_for: Teams that need published, independent benchmarks before adopting a model provider
Anyone depending on the frontier (Max / Lucia II) tier today — it has not opened
Buyers who require a vendor with an operating history and support organisation
Users who want a proven model and treat 'our own models' as a risk rather than a feature
red_flags: The product's entire advantage is proprietary models presented with no benchmarks, model cards or independent evaluation; 'no middleman / answerable to no third party' is unverifiable from the public surface — the free tier is the only way a buyer can judge quality, so treat it as mandatory before paying
A frontier tier (Lucia II / Max) is marketed as available-soon rather than shipped

compared_to.verdict_diff: Praex is a fork of opencode (MIT), so the client lineage is shared. opencode is model-agnostic and community-run; Praex adds its own hosted models, a phone/web surface and a paid tier. Choose opencode for a neutral, upstream client on models you choose; choose Praex if the multi-surface session and the bundled models earn their keep for you.

Claude Code is a terminal coding agent on a known, benchmarked frontier model with an established vendor; Praex offers more surfaces (phone, web) and a free everyday tier, but on models of unproven quality. Choose Claude Code when model quality and vendor track record are the priority; consider Praex when free multi-surface access and openness matter and you will judge the models yourself.

Codex pairs a well-known model with OpenAI's tooling and track record; Praex competes on openness, price (free to start) and reach across devices rather than on a proven model. The deciding question is whether you need a benchmarked model today or value the open, free, multi-surface shape more.

agent_relevance.agent_integration_path: Praex is itself a coding agent delivered as a CLI (single-line install) plus phone and web surfaces sharing one session. It can run on its own hosted models or on user-supplied keys. No separate programmatic API, MCP server or SDK for driving Praex from another agent is advertised on the captured surface; the client is open source (opencode fork, MIT), so integration would be at the fork level.
